investigation.title: Remote Agents: Swarm Gateway 502 Blocking All Agent Provisioning Evals
investigation.summary: All three remote-agents feature checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed at 2026-09-30T12:42–12:43Z with an identical 502 bad_gateway error indicating the swarm provisioning gateway — an AWS ELB in us-east-2 — was unreachable when the eval runner issued POST /api/agents. Because every sibling check shares the exact same error message and no evidence was collected, the failure is localized to the shared upstream swarm gateway dependency, not to any individual check's logic.
investigation.rootCause: The swarm gateway (an AWS ELB in us-east-2 fronting /v1/agents) was unreachable at the time of the eval run. The production-api layer returned HTTP 502 with code "bad_gateway" and the message "swarm gateway unreachable during agent provisioning" for every POST /api/agents call. Because all three remote-agents checks depend on a successful agent creation call through this gateway, all three failed before any evidence (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) could be collected. This is an eval-detected infrastructure availability signal; no user-traffic or incident data is present in the packet to confirm a broader production outage.

verifierContext.siblingCorrelation.likelySharedDependencyFailure: true — all failing sibling IDs share the same message
possibleCauses: The AWS ELB in us-east-2 serving the swarm /v1/agents endpoint was down, misconfigured, or had no healthy targets at the time of the eval run — most strongly supported by the 502 bad_gateway response and the identical failure across all three sibling checks.
A network routing or security-group change between the production-api layer and the ELB caused connection failures, producing the 502 at the API gateway layer before the swarm backend was reached.
The swarm backend service behind the ELB crashed or was restarting, causing the ELB to return 502 due to no healthy instances.
A transient infrastructure blip (deployment, scaling event, or AZ failover) in us-east-2 caused a brief window of unavailability that coincided with the eval run window (12:42–12:43Z).

whatWouldDisproveThis: A successful re-run of the remote-agent-create eval returning all four required evidence keys (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) would indicate the 502 was a transient blip rather than an ongoing gateway failure.
ELB access logs showing no inbound request from the production-api layer at 12:42–12:43Z would suggest the failure occurred before the ELB and implicate a network or DNS routing issue instead.
A passing result for remote-agent-create while remote-agent-state and remote-agent-runtime still fail would disprove the shared-dependency hypothesis and point to check-specific logic.

Evidence that POST /api/agents succeeds for local (non-remote) agent creation at the same timestamp would narrow the failure to the remote/swarm-specific provisioning path rather than the entire /api/agents route.
followUpEvals: Add a dedicated swarm-gateway-health eval that directly probes the ELB /v1/agents endpoint (or a health check route) independently of the full agent creation flow, so gateway-level failures are detected and reported separately from agent lifecycle failures.

Add a latency-regression eval for POST /api/agents that alerts when p95 latency approaches the warningLatencyMs=240000 threshold, providing earlier warning before a full 502 failure occurs.

Consider adding a retry-aware eval variant for remote-agent-create that retries once after a 502 and records whether the retry succeeded, distinguishing transient blips from sustained outages in the eval signal.

investigation.title: Remote Agents Feature: All Three Checks Failing with 502 Swarm Gateway Unreachable on POST /api/agents
investigation.summary: All three remote-agents observability checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed simultaneously at 2026-09-30T12:43Z with an identical 502 bad_gateway error indicating the swarm gateway backing POST /api/agents is unreachable. The eval runner's createAgent call (infra/evals/status/run-status-probes.mjs line 1905) never succeeded, so no agent was provisioned and zero required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) were collected, causing a complete contract gap.
investigation.rootCause: The swarm gateway — the AWS ELB-backed service at the redacted us-east-2 endpoint that handles POST /v1/agents — was unreachable at the time of the eval run. Because agent creation is the first step in the remote-agent-state probe (run-status-probes.mjs line 1905: createAgent), the 502 failure propagated immediately, preventing any downstream state polling and leaving all four required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) absent. The identical error message across all three sibling checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) confirms this is a shared upstream infrastructure failure, not an issue isolated to the remote-agent-state eval logic or its expected-output contract definition.

possibleCauses: Primary: The swarm gateway ELB in us-east-2 was down, misconfigured, or had no healthy targets at the time of the eval run, causing all POST /v1/agents requests to return 502. This is the strongest explanation given the identical error across all three sibling checks.

Secondary: A transient network partition or DNS resolution failure between the production-api runtime and the swarm gateway ELB caused a temporary inability to reach the endpoint, which may have self-resolved.

Tertiary: The swarm gateway ELB target group had zero healthy instances (e.g., due to a deployment, scaling event, or health-check failure) at the moment the evals ran, producing 502 responses for all agent provisioning requests.

Lower probability: A misconfigured or rotated endpoint URL for the swarm gateway in the production-api service configuration caused requests to be routed to an incorrect or decommissioned ELB address.

Review AWS ELB access logs and CloudWatch metrics for the redacted ELB endpoint around 2026-09-30T12:43Z to identify the duration and scope of the outage (e.g., zero healthy targets, connection resets, or upstream timeouts).

If the gateway is confirmed down or degraded, escalate to the team responsible for the swarm infrastructure in us-east-2 with the failure window (2026-09-30T12:43:00Z to at least 2026-09-30T12:43:22Z) and the specific ELB endpoint from the error message.
Once the gateway is restored, run the full remote-agents eval suite to confirm all three checks pass and all required evidence fields are collected.

recommendedVerifierProbes.reason: Checking the ELB target group health at the time of the failure (2026-09-30T12:43Z) and currently will confirm whether the gateway had healthy targets. Zero healthy targets would confirm the gateway-down hypothesis.

recommendedVerifierProbes.reason: Server-side logs will show whether the 502 originated from the ELB (no healthy targets) or from a connection-level failure (timeout, DNS, TLS), helping distinguish between a gateway-down and a network-partition scenario.

whatWouldDisproveThis: A successful re-run of the remote-agent-state eval returning all four required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) without any infrastructure change would suggest the original failure was a transient blip rather than a sustained gateway outage.

AWS ELB access logs showing the target group had healthy instances and was successfully serving requests at 2026-09-30T12:43Z would disprove a gateway-down hypothesis and shift focus to a network routing or authentication issue between production-api and the ELB.
A passing result for remote-agent-create while remote-agent-state fails would disprove the shared-dependency hypothesis and localize the fault to the state-polling logic specifically.

Evidence that the swarm gateway ELB endpoint URL changed or was decommissioned before the eval run, and that production-api was updated to reflect the new endpoint, would disprove a gateway-down scenario and instead implicate a configuration drift issue.
Logs from the production-api service showing the request to the ELB was never sent (e.g., a pre-flight auth or config failure) would disprove that the ELB itself was the failing component.
followUpEvals: Add a dedicated swarm-gateway-health eval that directly probes the ELB health endpoint (or a lightweight canary endpoint on /v1/agents) without requiring full agent provisioning, so gateway reachability failures are detected and reported independently of the agent lifecycle checks.

Add a gateway-reachability pre-flight check that runs before remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, and remote-agent-runtime, and short-circuits all three with a clear 'gateway unreachable' status rather than letting each check independently time out or fail with a 502.
Add a historical baseline to the remote-agents eval run history so that currentlyRegressedFromPass can be computed and regression alerts can fire when the checks transition from passing to failing.
Consider adding a latency-band eval for POST /api/agents that alerts when p95 latency approaches the warningLatencyMs threshold (240000ms), providing an early signal before full 502 failures occur.

investigation.summary: The eval for the published-observability-snapshot check failed because the snapshot at https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json was 693 minutes old at eval time (2026-09-30T12:43:25Z), more than double the 300-minute maximum asserted by the expected-output contract. All other public-website sibling checks passed, isolating the failure entirely to the staleness of the published snapshot JSON, not to any broader website or infrastructure outage.
investigation.rootCause: The GitHub Actions workflow responsible for regenerating and publishing the observability snapshot at https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json did not run successfully within the required 300-minute window. The snapshot served at eval time was approximately 11.5 hours old (693 minutes), indicating the scheduled or triggered workflow either did not fire, was queued and never executed, failed silently before publishing, or was cancelled. This is an eval-detected staleness condition scoped to the snapshot publication pipeline; no evidence of a user-facing website outage is present.
proof: failed-check.message: 'snapshotAgeMinutes expected <= 300 but got 693' — the sole violated assertion, confirmed by the eval runner at 2026-09-30T12:43:25.359Z.

failed-check.evidence: snapshotAgeMinutes=693, maxAgeMinutes=300, source='github-actions', hasLiveSource=true, generatedAtPresent=true — the snapshot is structurally valid and was produced by github-actions, but its age exceeds the contract ceiling by 393 minutes.
expected-output.contract: assertion { path: 'snapshotAgeMinutes', max: 300 } defined at infra/evals/status/check-expectations.json line 482 — this is the exact assertion that failed.

sibling.public-observability-page, sibling.public-models-page, sibling.public-marketing-pages: all three sibling checks passed with HTTP 200 responses, ruling out a shared infrastructure or hosting failure.
source.infra/evals/status/features.json:383: check config shows statusImpact='informational' and required=false, confirming this is an informational eval failure, not a required check outage.

source.infra/evals/status/run-status-probes.mjs:2168-2170: the runner fetches the live snapshot via publicJsonUrl(args.publishedSnapshotUrl) and derives snapshotAgeMinutes from the payload — the age value is read directly from the published artifact, not computed incorrectly by the runner.
possibleCauses: Most likely — The scheduled GitHub Actions workflow that publishes the observability snapshot did not execute or complete successfully within the past 300 minutes, leaving the previously published snapshot (693 minutes old) in place at the snapshotUrl.
Second — The GitHub Actions workflow ran but failed before the publish step (e.g., a build error, permissions issue, or upstream API timeout), so the old snapshot was never replaced.
Third — The GitHub Actions workflow was manually cancelled, paused, or its schedule was modified, causing a gap longer than 300 minutes between successful runs.

Fourth — A GitHub Pages deployment delay or caching layer caused the newly generated snapshot to not be visible at the snapshotUrl even if the workflow completed, though this is less likely given hasLiveSource=true and generatedAtPresent=true are both satisfied by the stale payload.
Least likely — A misconfiguration in the workflow trigger (e.g., cron expression, branch filter, or required secrets) silently prevented the workflow from being queued at all.

whatWouldDisproveThis: If a re-fetch of https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json shows snapshotAgeMinutes <= 300 at the time of the eval run, the staleness diagnosis would be disproved and the failure would instead point to a transient fetch or age-calculation error in the runner.

If GitHub Actions workflow run history shows a successful publish run completed within 300 minutes before 2026-09-30T12:43Z, the staleness would not be caused by a missed workflow run, and the cause would shift to a GitHub Pages caching or propagation delay.

If the snapshotAgeMinutes field in the published JSON is computed by the snapshot generator rather than derived by the eval runner from a generatedAt timestamp, and that computation contains a bug, the actual snapshot age could be less than 693 minutes — this would disprove the workflow-gap hypothesis.

If no GitHub Actions workflow exists for publishing the snapshot and the source field value 'github-actions' is set statically in the snapshot, the diagnosis of a missed workflow run would be incorrect.
followUpEvals: Add an eval that checks the GitHub Actions workflow run history directly and asserts the most recent successful run of the snapshot-publishing workflow completed within the last 240 minutes — providing a leading indicator before the snapshotAgeMinutes threshold is breached.

Add an eval that monitors the generatedAt timestamp in the published snapshot on a shorter polling interval (e.g., every 30 minutes) and emits a warning when snapshotAgeMinutes exceeds 180 minutes, giving earlier signal of a stalled workflow.

Add an eval that verifies the GitHub Actions workflow for snapshot publishing is enabled, has a valid schedule, and has at least one successful run in the past 24 hours — catching schedule misconfigurations before they produce stale snapshots.

Consider a regression eval that tracks snapshotAgeMinutes over consecutive runs to detect a monotonically increasing trend (indicating the workflow has stopped running) versus a one-time spike (indicating a transient delay).

investigations.title: Remote Agents: Swarm Gateway 502 Blocking All Agent Provisioning Evals
investigations.summary: All three remote-agents feature checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed at 2026-09-30T12:42–12:43Z with an identical 502 bad_gateway error indicating the swarm provisioning gateway — an AWS ELB in us-east-2 — was unreachable when the eval runner issued POST /api/agents. Because every sibling check shares the exact same error message and no evidence was collected, the failure is localized to the shared upstream swarm gateway dependency, not to any individual check's logic.
investigations.rootCause: The swarm gateway (an AWS ELB in us-east-2 fronting /v1/agents) was unreachable at the time of the eval run. The production-api layer returned HTTP 502 with code "bad_gateway" and the message "swarm gateway unreachable during agent provisioning" for every POST /api/agents call. Because all three remote-agents checks depend on a successful agent creation call through this gateway, all three failed before any evidence (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) could be collected. This is an eval-detected infrastructure availability signal; no user-traffic or incident data is present in the packet to confirm a broader production outage.

possibleCauses: The AWS ELB in us-east-2 serving the swarm /v1/agents endpoint was down, misconfigured, or had no healthy targets at the time of the eval run — most strongly supported by the 502 bad_gateway response and the identical failure across all three sibling checks.
A network routing or security-group change between the production-api layer and the ELB caused connection failures, producing the 502 at the API gateway layer before the swarm backend was reached.
The swarm backend service behind the ELB crashed or was restarting, causing the ELB to return 502 due to no healthy instances.
A transient infrastructure blip (deployment, scaling event, or AZ failover) in us-east-2 caused a brief window of unavailability that coincided with the eval run window (12:42–12:43Z).

investigations.summary: All three remote-agents observability checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed simultaneously at 2026-09-30T12:43Z with an identical 502 bad_gateway error indicating the swarm gateway backing POST /api/agents is unreachable. The eval runner's createAgent call (infra/evals/status/run-status-probes.mjs line 1905) never succeeded, so no agent was provisioned and zero required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) were collected, causing a complete contract gap.
investigations.rootCause: The swarm gateway — the AWS ELB-backed service at the redacted us-east-2 endpoint that handles POST /v1/agents — was unreachable at the time of the eval run. Because agent creation is the first step in the remote-agent-state probe (run-status-probes.mjs line 1905: createAgent), the 502 failure propagated immediately, preventing any downstream state polling and leaving all four required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) absent. The identical error message across all three sibling checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) confirms this is a shared upstream infrastructure failure, not an issue isolated to the remote-agent-state eval logic or its expected-output contract definition.

possibleCauses: Primary: The swarm gateway ELB in us-east-2 was down, misconfigured, or had no healthy targets at the time of the eval run, causing all POST /v1/agents requests to return 502. This is the strongest explanation given the identical error across all three sibling checks.

Secondary: A transient network partition or DNS resolution failure between the production-api runtime and the swarm gateway ELB caused a temporary inability to reach the endpoint, which may have self-resolved.

Tertiary: The swarm gateway ELB target group had zero healthy instances (e.g., due to a deployment, scaling event, or health-check failure) at the moment the evals ran, producing 502 responses for all agent provisioning requests.

Lower probability: A misconfigured or rotated endpoint URL for the swarm gateway in the production-api service configuration caused requests to be routed to an incorrect or decommissioned ELB address.

possibleCauses: Most likely — The scheduled GitHub Actions workflow that publishes the observability snapshot did not execute or complete successfully within the past 300 minutes, leaving the previously published snapshot (693 minutes old) in place at the snapshotUrl.
Second — The GitHub Actions workflow ran but failed before the publish step (e.g., a build error, permissions issue, or upstream API timeout), so the old snapshot was never replaced.
Third — The GitHub Actions workflow was manually cancelled, paused, or its schedule was modified, causing a gap longer than 300 minutes between successful runs.

Fourth — A GitHub Pages deployment delay or caching layer caused the newly generated snapshot to not be visible at the snapshotUrl even if the workflow completed, though this is less likely given hasLiveSource=true and generatedAtPresent=true are both satisfied by the stale payload.
Least likely — A misconfiguration in the workflow trigger (e.g., cron expression, branch filter, or required secrets) silently prevented the workflow from being queued at all.

If GitHub Actions workflow run history shows a successful publish run completed within 300 minutes before 2026-09-30T12:43Z, the staleness would not be caused by a missed workflow run, and the cause would shift to a GitHub Pages caching or propagation delay.

If the snapshotAgeMinutes field in the published JSON is computed by the snapshot generator rather than derived by the eval runner from a generatedAt timestamp, and that computation contains a bug, the actual snapshot age could be less than 693 minutes — this would disprove the workflow-gap hypothesis.

If no GitHub Actions workflow exists for publishing the snapshot and the source field value 'github-actions' is set statically in the snapshot, the diagnosis of a missed workflow run would be incorrect.
